title: Philadelphia Science Museum Closes as Supporters Seek a Way to Reopen
summary:
The Academy of Natural Sciences museum in Philadelphia closed on September 30. Founded in 1812, it opened to the public in 1828. In 1868, it became the first place in the world to display a dinosaur skeleton.

For many local families, visiting was a special tradition. Alexandria McCormick visited with her husband and six children. She said childhood visits helped her love nature. She felt sad that her children might miss similar experiences.

The Academy has more than 19 million specimens. A specimen is a sample of a plant, animal or fossil kept for study. The collection includes Thomas Jefferson's fossils and plant samples gathered by Lewis and Clark. Drexel University said students and researchers would keep access to the collection. Public access remains unclear.

Drexel took over financial responsibility for the Academy in 2011. It said costs rose and fewer people visited after the pandemic. When the closing was announced on September 1, thousands of families came for a final visit. In its last few weeks, museum revenue was more than 20 times higher than last September.

Some supporters criticized Drexel for the short notice and for not sharing the cost of keeping the museum open. Drexel said it remained committed to protecting the Academy's history and collections.

Before the closing, the William Penn Foundation offered funding for one year. This would give people time to explore lasting solutions. Drexel said it was exploring the offer but needed a long-term plan before considering reopening. Philadelphia's city council plans public hearings to learn how the closure happened and explore solutions.
why_it_matters: The closure affects a place where families learned about nature. Students and researchers will retain collection access, but public access and reopening remain uncertain.
